edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the packet id, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / PCFZV-K1-1", on every page.

edits.quote: Diagram: exactly 5 rows of 4 counters and exactly 8 rows of 5 counters
edits.fix: The number of printed rows gives away how many games there are (5 and 8), which removes the 'have we found them all?' thinking. Print a few extra rows (e.g. 7 and 10) so the child must decide when the list is complete.

edits.quote: If you go second, how can you win every time, whatever the other player does?
edits.fix: A K–1 child cannot write a 'how' answer and there is no recording space. Give a doable action: "You go second with two piles of 6. Find a way to win every game, whatever the other player does, and show it to your partner."

k-1.summary: A strong, concrete K–1 sequence: piles drawn as counters, traps found up to 20, a 1-2-3 rule change, two-pile games leading to the mirror strategy, and the last-counter-loses version, with every answer correct and enough work for forty minutes. Only light edits: the footer id, the pre-printed row count in Problem 6, and an answerable action for Problem 9.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the packet id, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / PCFZV-23-1", on every page.

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta narration: "Two players take turns taking counters from a pile." Keep the last-counter and cannot-move rules.

edits.quote: Mo says, “With 10 counters, I will go first and take 2, and then I can always win.”
edits.fix: The 10 row of Problem 1's table already settles Mo's claim. Use a pile beyond the table, e.g. "With 20 counters, I will go first and take 1" (wrong; taking 2 to leave 18 wins), so the child has to extend the pattern.

edits.quote: For each starting pile from 1 to 20, decide whether you would rather go first or second.
edits.fix: Delete; the next two sentences (shade / write your first move) already give the full task.

edits.quote: Four pairs (3,3), (4,2), (4,1), (4,4); "When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why."
edits.fix: This is thinner than the K–1 two-pile problem, and the follow-up points the child at the equal-pile case. Add more pairs (e.g. 5 and 2, 7 and 4, 5 and 5) and replace the follow-up with "Find two piles of different sizes where you would rather go second, and explain how the second player wins." (4 and 1 is one such pair.)

grades-2-3.summary: A well-built, mathematically correct sequence: claimed strategies tested against every reply, the {1, 3, 4} game classified and pushed to 100, a parity rule, inventing a rule that gives multiples of 5, and the last-counter-loses version. The edits are light: meta wording in the intro, a claim already settled by Problem 1, and a thin two-pile problem whose follow-up names the easy case.

edits.fix: Use the standard footer with the packet id, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / PCFZV-45-1", on every page.

edits.quote: In every game in this packet, two players take turns taking counters from a pile. Each problem says how many counters a player may take on a turn.
edits.fix: Cut the meta narration: "Two players take turns taking counters from a pile." Keep the last-counter and cannot-move rules, which Problem 6 needs.

edits.quote: For each starting pile from 1 to 24, decide whether you would rather go first or second.
edits.fix: Delete; the shade / write-your-move sentences already state the task.

edits.quote: "A starting pile where you would rather go second is called a losing pile. Every other starting pile is a winning pile." / "From now on, a game is named by its list of allowed moves, so the game in Problem 1 is the {1, 3, 4} game."
edits.fix: Both are activity-wide definitions used in every later problem. State them once in the shared rules at the top and start P2 and P3 with their tasks.

edits.quote: When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why.
edits.fix: For 4–5 this asks only about the diagonal, which the K–1 band already does. The grid shows much more (second player wins exactly when the piles leave the same remainder on division by 3). Replace with "Describe which squares are shaded and explain why the second player wins from them."

grades-4-5.summary: The strongest band: it classifies {1, 3, 4}, extends it to 2026, compares rules, refutes the greedy plan, asks for a periodicity proof, asks for every move set from 1 to 6 whose losing piles are the multiples of 4, and covers the last-counter-loses version and two-pile grids. Every answer checks out. The edits are light: move the definitions into the shared rules, trim the intro and one redundant sentence, and replace Problem 8's equal-piles follow-up with the full remainder pattern.

overall.strongest: The grades 4–5 band develops all three outline kernels (classification, repeating patterns with proof, rule changes and greedy failure, two-pile games) through a well-chosen, correct sequence.
overall.weakest: The grades 2–3 two-pile problem is thinner than the K–1 version and its follow-up points the child at the easy equal-pile case.
